analysis.one_liner: Raises the base minimum wage for tipped workers from $2.13 toward $5.50 an hour.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise tipped workers' base pay never got a vote; it sat in a House committee until the 2011-2012 Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, tipped workers like servers can be paid as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages, with tips expected to make up the rest. This bill would have stepped that base wage up to $3.75, then $5.00, then 70% of the regular minimum wage (at least $5.50). It was introduced with 34 Democratic cosponsors, referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee, and never received a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly four million Americans work for tips, most of them restaurant servers, bartenders, and salon workers. Raising their required cash wage means a steadier paycheck that does not depend entirely on customers' generosity, and it narrows the gap they must cover with tips to reach the full minimum wage. Women make up a large share of tipped workers and would be among the biggest gainers.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a federal base cash wage for tipped employees of $3.75 an hour 90 days after enactment, up from $2.13.
Raises it again to $5.00 an hour one year later, then to 70% of the regular minimum wage, never less than $5.50, two years after that.
Requires the Labor Department to publish public notice of each scheduled tipped-wage increase before it takes effect.
Under existing law, if tips plus the cash wage fall short of the full minimum wage, the employer must make up the difference; a higher base wage reduces how much depends on that underenforced rule.

analysis.who_pays: Restaurants, bars, and other businesses that employ tipped workers would pay higher hourly wages, raising their labor costs. Some employers would pass costs to customers through higher prices or menu fees; the industry argued others would cut hours or jobs. Restaurant chains and their lobby groups opposed raising the tipped minimum.

drawbacks.text: The bill phases in over several years and its final floor, 70% of the minimum wage (no less than $5.50), still leaves tipped workers' base pay below the regular minimum wage, so it is a partial fix rather than eliminating the two-tier wage.

Employers in labor-intensive food service would face materially higher payroll costs; opponents argued this could lead to fewer hours, higher prices, or slower hiring, especially for small independent restaurants.
Because the raise is scheduled years out, the benefit to workers arrives slowly rather than as an immediate increase.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest by design: a higher guaranteed cash wage for workers whose pay currently rests almost entirely on tips, phased in over several years at a level still below the regular minimum. The main cost falls on food service employers, some of whom could offset it through prices. The bigger criticism is that the bill does too little, too slowly, not that it does harm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended in January 2013, without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Donna Edwards introduced the WAGES Act on February 10, 2011, with 12 original cosponsors including Reps. Grijalva, McGovern, Nadler, Baldwin, and Norton.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
A month later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was ever recorded.
The committee never reported the bill, so it never reached the House floor for a vote in the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tipped workers gained nothing. Employers of tipped workers and the restaurant industry kept the $2.13 base wage in place, and House leaders avoided a vote that would have forced members on record.

for.name: Rep. Donna F. Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the WAGES Act and recruited 34 cosponsors for it.

for.name: 34 of 193 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republicans signed on.

against.name: Rep. John Kline
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it in subcommittee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Restaurant industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising the tipped minimum wage, keeping the $2.13 base intact.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would raise the cash wage restaurants must pay their roughly 2.5 million-plus tipped servers and bartenders, increasing payroll costs. Under the current system, customers' tips substitute for wages, so the industry's interest in keeping the $2.13 base runs against the workers it employs.
Salons and other tipped-service employers would pay the higher base wage. Like restaurants, their pay structure depends on tips replacing wages.
